extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of stationary combustion turbines, regulated industry, state/federal permitting authorities, and environmental/regulatory stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance for applicability, subcategorization, and standards-of-performance (BSER) for new and reconstructed stationary combustion turbines under 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTTa, including criteria for CHP treatment, design-efficiency calculation, electric-sales thresholds, and BSER determinations by subcategory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability exclusions for certain combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific types of units are not subject to the standard: (1) units capable of deriving >=50% of heat input from non-fossil fuel at base load and subject to federally enforceable permit limiting annual capacity factor for all fossil fuels combined to 10% or less; (2) combined heat and power (CHP) units subject to a federally enforceable permit limiting annual net electric sales to no more than 219,000 MWh or the product of design efficiency and potential electric output, whichever is greater; (3) units serving a generator along with other steam generating units, IGCC, or stationary combustion turbines where the effective generation capacity is 25 MW or less; (4) municipal waste combustors subject to 40 CFR part 60, subpart Eb; (5) commercial/industrial solid waste incineration units subject to 40 CFR part 60, subpart CCCC; and (6) units deriving >50% of heat input from an industrial process that does not produce any electrical or mechanical output used outside the affected stationary combustion turbine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated exclusions define narrowly scoped source types that fall outside subpart TTTTa applicability. The preamble lists these explicitly as categories the Agency treated as not subject to the new standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability in non-continental and non-contiguous areas
rubrics_metrics.description: For combustion turbines located in non-continental areas (Hawaii, Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, Northern Mariana Islands) and non-contiguous areas (non-continental areas and Alaska), only the initial BSER component will be applicable to owners/operators; owners/operators of base load combustion turbines in non-contiguous areas will not be subject to the CCS-based numerical standards in 2032 and will continue to comply with an efficiency-based numeric standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA is finalizing limited applicability for these geographies due to differences from the contiguous 48 states and limited recent/new construction in those areas; the Agency retains authority to amend this in future rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: CHP unit net electric sales and applicability (elimination of 20% output restriction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under subpart TTTTa, EPA is eliminating the restriction that CHP units must produce at least 20.0 percent electrical or mechanical output to qualify for the CHP-specific method of calculating net electric sales and net energy output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a CHP unit with less than 20% electric output meets the other applicability criteria, net electric sales and net energy output are calculated the same as for a traditional non-CHP EGU. The change removes the previous 20% floor so more CHP configurations can use the CHP-specific calculation method where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on subtracting host facility purchased power for third-party CHP developers
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party CHP units may subtract purchased power of the thermal host facility when determining net electric sales, but the amount that can be subtracted is limited to the percentage of useful thermal output provided to the host facility by the specific CHP unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation prevents double-counting of host purchased power when multiple third-party developers serve the same thermal host and prevents trivial thermal sales to multiple hosts being used to inappropriately subtract purchased power. For avoidance of double counting, purchased power subtraction must be prorated based on the fraction of thermal output actually provided by the CHP unit to each host.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of exemption for stationary combustion turbines not capable of combusting natural gas
rubrics_metrics.description: Subpart TTTTa does not include the prior exemption for turbines that are not physically capable of combusting natural gas (e.g., not connected to a natural gas pipeline). Such units meet general applicability and are subject to requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners/operators burning fuels with higher heat-input emission rates than natural gas must adjust the natural-gas-fired emissions rate by the ratio of the heat-input-based emission rates (lb CO2/MMBtu basis). The practical effect is these units must maintain equivalent efficiency relative to a natural-gas-fired turbine and comply with the BSER-identified standard of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategorization by electric sales (low/intermediate/base load) on monthly and rolling-average bases
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing three subcategories—low load, intermediate load, and base load combustion turbines—determined based on electric sales (utilization) relative to the turbine's potential electric output on both a 12-operating month and 3-year rolling average basis. Subcategory determination is performed each operating month and units may switch subcategories when operation changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electric sales (percent of potential electric output) is used as a proxy for operational behavior (starts/stops, duty cycle) and thus for determining appropriate BSER and performance standards. This monthly, rolling-average approach allows subcategory membership to reflect actual operational patterns over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of electric sales (percent electric sales) as the subcategorization metric (rather than heat-input capacity factor or annual hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA uses percent electric sales relative to potential electric output as the basis for subcategorization because it reflects operational limitations inherent in unit design and is relevant to which emission reduction technologies are suitable for different units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electric sales better captures the way turbines are used (peaking vs base load) and aligns with industry practices (e.g., permits with annual operating hour limits). The Agency found this approach appropriate for NSPS purposes and for determining BSER across subcategories.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER determination by subcategory: low load — lower-emitting fuels
rubrics_metrics.description: For low load (peaking) combustion turbines with highly variable operation and emission rates, the BSER is limited to the use of lower-emitting fuels (e.g., natural gas and Nos. 1 and 2 fuel oils).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because low load turbines operate with frequent starts/stops and short run-times, their emissions are highly variable and it is difficult to establish a meaningful output-based performance standard; therefore EPA limited BSER to low-emitting fuel use for this subcategory.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER determination by subcategory: intermediate load — efficient design and operation
rubrics_metrics.description: For intermediate load combustion turbines (those operating at somewhat higher loads than peaking units) EPA determined that efficient design and operation is the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermediate load units often are simple cycle turbines that start and stop relatively frequently; CCS is impracticable for many of these units due to lack of HRSG, so improvements in efficiency/design/operation are the appropriate BSER for this subcategory.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER determination by subcategory: base load — highly efficient combined cycle generation (and CCS practicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: For base load combustion turbines, BSER is based on highly efficient combined cycle generation; CCS is practicable for combined cycle turbines that operate at relatively high loads and thus is an appropriate control technology for base load units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EPA focused BSER for base load units on combined cycle technology because these units have steady-state operation, higher efficiency, and are better suited for CCS. The Agency evaluated emissions data for combined cycle turbines with 12-operating month capacity factors >=40% in setting standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design efficiency calculated on HHV basis and default to gross output for standards; optional net-output equivalents and auxiliary load conversions
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing that design efficiency for calculating potential electric output will be based on higher heating value (HHV) rather than lower heating value (LHV). Most emissions data and output-based standards are based on gross output; EPA is including optional equivalent standards on a net-output basis and used auxiliary load conversions of 2% for simple and combined cycle turbines and 7% for combined cycle EGUs using 90% CCS to convert between bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HHV yields a larger heat input and thus lower HHV efficiency relative to LHV; the Agency's default is HHV to reference technologies consistently. Manufacturers often report LHV; the rule explains conversion and offers optional net-output equivalents to recognize minimizing auxiliary loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of sliding-scale design-efficiency caps and adoption of fixed electric-sales thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is eliminating the prior sliding-scale electric-sales threshold that relied on design efficiency (including the 50% maximum and 33% minimum restrictions) and is instead finalizing fixed percent electric sales thresholds; the design efficiency will no longer affect subcategorization thresholds (though design efficiency is still used to determine potential electric sales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing the 33% minimum and 50% maximum avoids reducing incentives to develop higher-efficiency turbines. EPA finalized a fixed threshold between intermediate and base load of 40% (see separate metric). This decision decouples subcategorization thresholds from manufacturer-reported design efficiency variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed electric-sales threshold between intermediate and base load: 40 percent
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA finalized a fixed electric sales (capacity factor) threshold of 40 percent as the threshold between intermediate load combustion turbines and base load combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 40% threshold reflects the maximum capacity factor for intermediate load simple cycle turbines and the minimum practical threshold for base load combined cycle turbines; EPA found combined cycle EGUs have lower LCOE than simple cycle EGUs above ~40% capacity factor, supporting the threshold and BSER selection for base load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination and rationale for low-load threshold (evaluated thresholds and emission-rate stability)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluated low/intermediate threshold candidates of 10%, 15%, 20%, and 25% capacity factors and concluded that a 10% threshold is problematic because simple cycle turbines operating at <=10% have highly variable emission rates and most new simple cycle turbines operate above 10%. EPA observed that GHG emission rates for many simple cycle turbines begin to stabilize at capacity factors above 15%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analytic basis (emission-rate variability and distribution of actual turbine capacity factors) informs the finalized low vs intermediate subcategory split. EPA's analysis of recent installation data (percentiles cited) also informed the chosen threshold to avoid subjecting many new simple cycles to an impracticable intermediate-load standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategory membership determination timing and switching
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicability to a subcategory is determined each operating month and a stationary combustion turbine can switch subcategories if the owner/operator changes how the facility is operated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both a 12-operating month and a 3-year rolling average basis are used for subcategory determination. This monthly determination allows standards to track operational reality and provides flexibility as unit usage changes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale re: operational behavior (starts/stops) and control technology suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric sales subcategorization recognizes operational differences (e.g., starts/stops, duty cycles) across turbine types—combined cycle, frame simple cycle, aeroderivative simple cycle—that affect emission rates and the suitability/practicability of emission reduction technologies (e.g., CCS works better at base load steady-state operation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA reviewed empirical start/operation statistics and found key capacity-factor thresholds where starts per unit and hours per start change markedly; these operational characteristics inform which technologies are feasible and effective for each subcategory and underlie BSER choices.
